title: Where Did the Ark Come to Rest?

regions.label: Ararat (Urartu)
regions.note: "The mountains of Ararat" (8:4) is a land, not one peak: Urartu of the Assyrian records, a kingdom of the highlands around Lake Van from the 9th to the 6th century BC. Sennacherib's sons fled "to the land of Ararat" (2 Kings 19:37), and Jeremiah summons "the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz" against Babylon (51:27).
Kardu or Qardu, the mountains south of Lake Van above the Tigris, where the Aramaic and Syriac translations and Berossus put the ark.
The Assyrian heartland on the Tigris, whose records name Urartu, Nimush and Kardu.
Western Anatolia, home of the Apamea tradition.

groups.name: Proposed resting places of the ark

places.m: Ağrı Dağı (Armenian Masis), eastern Turkey · 5,137 m
places.note: The highest peak in the region, a snow-capped volcano. Genesis says only "the mountains of Ararat"; the name Mount Ararat was given to this peak by Armenian tradition from about the 11th century, and medieval travellers such as William of Rubruck and Marco Polo knew it as the ark's mountain. It is the traditional site today.

places.m: near Üzengili, Doğubayazıt, Turkey · about 29 km south of Ağrı Dağı
places.note: A boat-shaped formation about 160 m long, exposed after earthquakes in 1948 and noticed in aerial photographs in 1959. Ron Wyatt promoted it as the ark from 1977, and Turkey opened a visitor centre there. Geologists who have studied it, including the 1960 expedition, describe it as a natural formation.

places.m: Cudi Dağı, Şırnak province, south-eastern Turkey · 2,089 m
places.note: The oldest named tradition. Berossus (3rd century BC, quoted by Josephus) put the ark in the mountains of the Kordyaeans, Gordyene; the Aramaic Targum Onkelos and the Syriac Peshitta read "the mountains of Qardu" in Genesis 8:4; and the Quran says the ark "came to rest on al-Judi" (11:44). Syriac Christians had a monastery on the mountain, and travellers into the Middle Ages were shown the place of the ark here.

Josephus says the Armenians showed "the Place of Descent," where Noah came out of the ark (Antiquities 1.92). Armenian tradition later explained the name Nakhchivan as "the place of first descent," and Noah's tomb is still shown in the city.

A Phrygian tradition: the Sibylline Oracles place the ark's mountain near the springs of the Marsyas at Celaenae. The city was nicknamed Kibotos, "the Ark," and its coins of the 3rd century AD show Noah and his wife in the ark, with the name NΩE and the dove.

places.m: Takht-e Suleyman, Alborz mountains, Iran · 4,659 m
places.note: A modern proposal: in 2006 Bob Cornuke's BASE Institute reported a blackened, beam-like rock formation high on this mountain. Critics showed that the 1894 account the search relied on describes a different Takht-i-Suliman, in Baluchistan, and the claim has found little support.

places.m: Pira Magrun (Pir Omar Gudrun), Iraqi Kurdistan · 2,611 m
places.note: In the Babylonian flood story (Gilgamesh, tablet XI), Utnapishtim's boat comes to rest on Mount Nimush, once read Nisir, and after seven days he sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven. The annals of Ashurnasirpal II place Nimush east of the Lesser Zab, and it is usually identified with Pira Magrun near Sulaymaniyah.

p: Genesis does not name a mountain. The ark came to rest "on the mountains of Ararat" (8:4), and the tops of the mountains appeared only two and a half months later (8:5). Ararat is the Hebrew name of Urartu, the highland kingdom around Lake Van, so the text points to a region rather than a single summit.

Over the centuries Jews, Christians and Muslims have pointed to different peaks within or near that region. The oldest named tradition is Mount Judi (Qardu) south of Lake Van; Mount Ararat, the great volcano to the north, became the usual site in the Middle Ages. The Book of Jubilees names "Lubar, one of the mountains of Ararat" (5:28), which has not been identified.

Red marks are places proposed for the ark's landing, with their names today. Faint marks are later or weakly supported proposals. The black mark is the landing place in the Babylonian flood story, for comparison. Tap a mark for its history.
